Computing FIRST and FOLLOW every time would be slow. Better to write down the answers first.
That answer sheet, with one cell per pair, is the LL(1) table.
The table recipe has two rules and a warning.
X goes to epsilon went into the closing parenthesis column. Tap the rule that did that.
Epsilon vanishes. Then what comes after X is in charge.
Right. Rule two: the FOLLOW columns.
A list of ids separated by commas. Now you fill it in.
Tap the cell where L goes to id R goes.
It starts with id. Use rule one.
Right. The id column.
R goes to comma, id, R. Tap its cell.
It starts with the comma.
Right. The comma column.
R can also vanish. The FOLLOW of R is just the dollar sign. Tap the cell.
Rule two: epsilon goes in the FOLLOW columns.
Right. R vanishes when the input ends.
No cell with two rules. This grammar is LL(1).
1. A → α goes in the columns of the FIRST of α.
2. If α vanishes, it also goes in the FOLLOW of A.
Warning: two rules in one cell, not LL(1).
The parser pushed E and plus. It needs to remember which rule it's in.
Without that, it wouldn't know if it expects an n or can already reduce.
A rule with a dot marking what was already read is an item.
The recipe for building the states has two operations.
Dot before E. Which operation pulls in the rules of E? Tap it.
It's the one that looks at the symbol right after the dot.
Right. Closure.
After the goto, always do the closure again.
Another grammar: parentheses around id. Start with state zero.
In state zero, the dot is before S. Which items does the closure pull in? Tap both.
The dot sits at the start of the rules of S.
Right. The two items with the dot at the start.
From state zero, reading id, where does the dot go? Tap the item.
The dot jumps over the id.
Right. Dot at the end: this state reduces.
Reading an opening parenthesis, the dot lands before S. Does it need a closure?
A dot before a nonterminal always pulls in its rules.
Right. The rules of S come in again.
The states are ready. Where the dot reaches the end, the table will reduce.
1. Closure: a dot before A pulls in the rules of A.
2. Goto: move the dot and close again.
3. Dot at the end: the state can reduce.

The state has E goes to n, with the dot at the end. Reduce now?
If the next token can't come after E, reducing goes wrong.
SLR, the simple LR, decides to reduce by looking at FOLLOW.
The SLR table recipe has three rules.
State two has E goes to n, dot. Which rule fills its row? Tap it.
The dot is at the end of the rule.
Right. Rule two: reduce in the FOLLOW columns.
Rule three: the start symbol's item with the dot at the end accepts the input.
Now parentheses around id. The state has S goes to id, dot.
The FOLLOW of S has closing parenthesis and dollar sign. Tap the reduce cells.
Rule two: only in the FOLLOW columns.
Right. In the other columns, the cell stays empty.
After id, the next token is an opening parenthesis. Tap what the table does.
The opening parenthesis cell stayed empty.
Right. An empty cell is a syntax error.
With the right FOLLOW, the table reduces only where the rule can end.
1. Goto on terminal t: s in column t.
2. A → α •: r in the FOLLOW columns of A.
3. S' → S •: ok in the dollar sign column.

Some grammars have a FOLLOW that says reduce where it shouldn't.
The problem: FOLLOW applies to every state at once.
LR(1) writes on each item which token can come after.
Here are four LR(1) items. After the comma comes the expected token.
The LALR recipe has two steps.
Which step makes the table small again? Tap it.
It's the step that merges states.
Right. Merging equal cores shrinks the table.
The result reduces by mistake less often than SLR.
Two LR(1) states from another grammar. Compare them.
Which two have the same core? Tap them.
Ignore the token after the comma.
Right. Same rule, same dot.
Merged, which tokens does the item get? Tap the right box.
Join the tokens of both.
Right. Closing parenthesis and dollar sign in the same item.
That's how LALR stays small without losing the token's precision.
1. Build the LR(1) states, with tokens.
2. Merge equal cores and join the tokens.
Result: SLR size, fewer conflicts.
This automaton has four states. Maybe two of them do the same thing.
Which of these states is final? Tap it.
A final state has a double circle.
Right. D is the only final one.
States that accept and reject the same words can become one.
Merging equivalent states makes the automaton minimal, with the same result.
The tool is the table of pairs. Each cell compares two states.
The recipe has three steps and repeats until it stops.
I marked A with B because they go to C and D. Tap the rule I used.
It wasn't because one is final. It was because of where they go.
Right. Rule two, by destination.
Stop only when a whole round marks nothing.
Another automaton: P, Q and R, with R final.
Tap the pairs the first rule marks.
Look for the pairs with R, which is final.
Right. Only R is final. The other two aren't.
P and Q, on zero, both go to Q. On one, to R. Merge or split?
The destinations are the same. No marked pair shows up.
Right. The two become a single state.
Two states are left. The automaton accepts the same words as before.
merge
split
1. Mark every final with non-final pair.
2. Mark the pair that goes to a marked pair.
3. Repeat until nothing changes. Blank: merge.
The parser built the parse tree. It's huge.
The next phases only need to know the operation and its two sides.
The tree with only the operation and its sides is the abstract syntax tree.
The recipe for building the AST has three rules.
In the tree, each name became a leaf. Which rule is that? Tap it.
A name has no children.
Right. Rule two: values and names become leaves.
Rule three: the parenthesis already did its job. It vanishes.
Now build the AST for total times, open parenthesis, price minus two.
Which operator goes at the root? Tap it.
The parenthesis makes the minus happen first. Whatever comes last is the root.
Right. Times is the last operation, so it goes at the root.
The minus sits under the times. What are the minus's children? Tap them.
They're the two sides of the minus.
Right. Price and two are leaves of the minus.
No parentheses in the tree, and the order is still right.
1. An operator becomes a node; operands become children.
2. A value or a name becomes a leaf.
3. Parentheses and pass-through rules vanish.
The processor doesn't know variables. It knows registers and memory.
Math only happens between registers, inside the processor.
MIPS is a simple machine for practicing this translation.
The recipe for each three-address line has three steps.
Which step brings the values from memory? Tap it.
The processor only adds what's already in a register.
Right. The lw comes first.
Rule three: without the sw, the result is lost when the register gets reused.
Now price plus tax. The lines are out of order.
Tap the two lines that come first.
Before adding, the values have to be in registers.
Right. The two lw's open the trio.
And which line closes the trio? Tap it.
The result has to go back to memory.
Right. The sw stores the result.
Now you can translate any simple sum to MIPS.
1. lw: load each operand into a register.
2. Math between registers: add, sub, mul.
3. sw: store the result in memory.
